entries.summary: ruby2shell lets attackers corrupt memory in default Rails and Sinatra apps without logging in. Cloudflare WAF blocks it for every customer, including Free plans.
entries.text: On November 19, 2026, the Ruby team disclosed ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825), a heap buffer overflow in the way Ruby changes the case of strings. Ruby rates the flaw Critical and says it is aware of proofs of concept that achieve remote code execution in some scenarios. Fixes shipped in Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10. The reach is wide. Veria Labs reports that Ruby on Rails and classic-style Sinatra applications reach the bug in their default configuration, before any authentication. Self-hosted products that bundle Ruby, including GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, OpenProject, Discourse and Chatwoot, shipped an affected Ruby in their latest release at the time of disclosure. Cloudflare WAF blocks ruby2shell for all customers, including those on the Free plan. We have added two rules to both the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, with Block as the default action: one for ruby2shell and one for GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, a related integer overflow in Ruby string case conversion fixed in the same releases. The WAF is a compensating control, not a replacement for patching. Exploits can reach the bug through paths a WAF does not see, and the only complete fix is to upgrade Ruby. Our team continues to monitor attack traffic and will update the rules as new techniques appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and get the latest on the vulnerability in the Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing. Cloudflare has patched its own systems that use
entries.title: How Cloudflare WAF protects against ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825)

entries.summary: phpAfterShell is a critical flaw in PHP's default session handler that can lead to code execution.
entries.text: On November 19, 2026, the security research company depthfirst disclosed phpAfterShell (CVE-2026-126714), a vulnerability in PHP's default file-based session handler that can lead to remote code execution. Under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 4.0, it scores 9.2 out of 10 (Critical). The PHP project fixed it the same day in versions 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, and 8.6.0. These releases fix 16 other security vulnerabilities, six of them also rated critical. Cloudflare’s web application firewall (WAF) blocks known phpAfterShell attack patterns, including for customers on the Free plan. The protection comes from a PHP remote code execution rule we first deployed in October 2026 for the php2shell vulnerabilities. That rule already detected part of the phpAfterShell attack pattern before the vulnerability was disclosed, and on November 19 we updated its detection logic to cover phpAfterShell. The rule is part of both the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, is enabled by default, and its default action is Block. In the same WAF release, we added three new rules to the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset for paid plans: one for a request smuggling flaw in PHP-FPM (CVE-2026-129289), and two for flaws in PHP's SOAP extension (CVE-2026-15353 and CVE-2026-129506) that PHP fixed in the same releases. These rules are enabled by default with the Log action, because the request patterns they look for can also appear in legitimate traffic, and blocki
entries.title: How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against phpAfterShell and other critical PHP flaws

entries.summary: Five memory corruption bugs in nginx, called nginx2root, can let an unauthenticated attacker run code on a server.
entries.text: On November 18, 2026, F5 and nginx.org disclosed ten vulnerabilities in nginx. Five of them, detailed by the Xint research team and published under the name nginx2root, are memory corruption flaws that an unauthenticated attacker can use to crash an nginx worker or, per Xint's research, run commands on the server. Xint also found a Linux kernel bug that turns that foothold into root on the host, including from inside a Docker container. Other teams found the two HTTP/2 bugs independently: F5 also credits Rapid7, Wiz Research and Ikotas Labs for CVE-2026-123007, and Metnir, Wiz Research, and Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 for CVE-2026-123633. nginx is an HTTP web server that also serves as reverse proxy, content cache, load balancer, TCP/UDP proxy server, and mail proxy server. nginx runs a large share of the world's web servers, so this is a patch-now event. But if your nginx server is reachable only through Cloudflare's proxy, attackers cannot reach the vulnerable code paths for the most serious of these bugs, giving you protection while you update your servers. Here is where Cloudflare stands, what that protection covers, where it stops, and how the bugs work. The short version Cloudflare's edge is not affected. Much of the proxy that handles customer traffic at our edge now runs on FL2, written in Rust. We reviewed the parts still built on our heavily modified nginx fork against all five bugs before disclosure, and an update closing the related code paths finished rolling out
entries.title: nginx2root: Five new nginx vulnerabilities, and how Cloudflare protects origins from the worst of them

entries.summary: On November 3, 2026 U.S. voters headed to the polls. Here’s what Cloudflare data across more than 1,400 protected sites tells us about Election Day Internet traffic and cyberattacks.
entries.text: Visitors to government election websites surged 363% on November 3, the date of the 2026 midterm elections in the United States. Across Cloudflare's election protection programs, we also detected a significant shift in the types and timing of cyberattacks throughout 2026. Unlike what we saw in other recent elections, attackers focused on gaining access to internal systems and data, rather than knocking websites offline. Government election websites faced website vulnerability attempts 180 times more often than denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, and at roughly ten times the rate of Cloudflare's broader customer base. We also found evidence of at least one attempt to exploit a recently disclosed critical PHP vulnerability on a state government voting website in the Western United States. These attacks peaked in late October, several weeks before the election. Vulnerability exploit attempts climbed steadily throughout 2026: from 200,000 per day in January, to 2 million per day in October. However, on Election Day in the U.S., Cloudflare detected no escalation in attack volume and zero major DDoS incidents across protected election sites, marking a sharp contrast to other recent elections, such as in Moldova last year. Our data regarding cyberattacks on election institutions came from organizations participating in Cloudflare's free cybersecurity programs: the Athenian Project, Cloudflare for Campaigns, and Project Galileo. Together, these initiatives helped protect more than 1,40
entries.title: Internet traffic and attacks during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections

Both extraction models are hosted on Workers AI and full open weights are available on Hugging Face. This team is working quickly to push the AI frontier and build useful models for Cloudflare’s customers and the open source community. A new version of Clairic: redesigned after the preview release Since announcing Clairic in preview, we have received a ton of use cases and helpful feedback on how customers wanted to use an extraction model. We heard about use cases ranging from extracting data from images like receipts to reading values from support tickets. We knew that we wanted extraction to be the clear focus for the model, so it had to excel at reading from unstructured data. We decided to go back to the d
entries.title: An updated Clairic and Clairic-flash are now open-weight, from the new Workers AI Superintelligence team

entries.summary: Java4Shell is a critical memory-corruption flaw in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder that can lead to remote code execution. Cloudflare has released six WAF managed rules for paid plans that logs matching requests by default.
entries.text: On November 17, 2026, the security research company Calif disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption vulnerability in the Base64 decoder of OpenJDK, the most widely used Java runtime. Under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 4.0, it scores 9.2 out of 10 (Critical). The flaw affects Java. OpenJDK published a security advisory and Oracle released patched builds in its November 2026 Critical Patch Update the same day, at 21:00 UTC. The vulnerability lets a remote attacker with no credentials send malformed Base64 data to a Java application and overwrite memory next to the decoded output. Calif turned that overwrite into a leak of heap memory, similar to Heartbleed, and into remote code execution. Calif demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution against Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate in their default configurations, and post-authentication remote code execution against Apache Kafka, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker. Cloudflare has released a new set of rules in the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset designed to detect malformed Base64 input patterns associated with this vulnerability. The rules are available on Pro, Business and Enterprise plans and are enabled by default with the Log action because malformed input and some benign application-specific token formats can resemble exploitation attempts. Blocking by default could therefore disrupt legitimate traffic. Customer
entries.title: How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)

entries.summary: Quad9's forced withdrawal from France highlights the dangers of mandating DNS-level blocking. We explore why forcing public resolvers to act as content filters is technically flawed and threatens the open Internet.
entries.text: Last month, the Swiss non-profit foundation Quad9 announced that it will withdraw its free public DNS resolver from France. This difficult decision followed months of litigation and a French court ruling that imposed daily financial penalties on Quad9 for failing to block domains associated with alleged copyright infringement. Quad9’s departure from France is both disheartening and understandable. The court’s ruling put the organization in the impossible bind of having to choose between crippling litigation and penalties, or fundamentally altering its service in a way that would undermine the privacy and security of its users. Left with no good option, Quad9 is choosing the exit door instead. The withdrawal of a basic infrastructure service from France fundamentally harms the free and open Internet, and it should serve as a warning of the damage that will result if rightsholders and policymakers continue demanding maximal blocking across every layer of the Internet. It not only deprives French Internet users of a trustworthy and important tool; it creates a real risk of disruption to their daily lives. Quad9’s resolver is used by a wide variety of individuals and organizations in France — including government bodies, educational institutions, hospitals, and utilities — and Quad9 has no way to directly notify those individuals and institutions that their resolver will soon stop working. If the affected parties do not change their resolver before Quad9 removes its service, thei
entries.title: Quad9’s withdrawal from France: A canary in the coal mine

entries.summary: Kitesurf, our experimental browser engine for AI agents, is now open source. Inspect the code, run it locally, or deploy your own instance on Cloudflare Workers.
entries.text: We introduced Kitesurf, our stateless browser for AI agents that runs entirely on top of Workers, in August and followed up in September with WebMCP support, new APIs, and improved compatibility. On every occasion, we mentioned our commitment to open sourcing it so that developers could run their own browser engine on their own Cloudflare accounts if they want to. That promise is now real. Kitesurf is open source on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. You can read the code, run it locally, change it, and deploy your own instance to Cloudflare Workers. A browser built for agents Kitesurf runs entirely on Cloudflare Workers. It parses HTML, applies CSS, executes page JavaScript, and renders screenshots without a browser container. It supports the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), so you can connect clients such as Puppeteer. Our main goal is to give AI agents a lightweight, efficient browser — one that can load websites, execute JavaScript, and interact with pages while using less CPU and memory than a full browser like Chromium, and scaling on demand across Cloudflare’s global Workers network. Read more about why and how we built Kitesurf in our initial announcement and how to use it in Browser Run’s developer documentation. What is inside the repository? Kitesurf builds on Cloudflare’s Developer Platform and APIs, alongside an ecosystem of open-source Rust packages compiled to WebAssembly: Blitz provides HTML parsing, the DOM, layout, and painting. Stylo provides CSS parsing,
entries.title: Kitesurf is now open source

entries.summary: AI-orchestrated penetration testing platforms like ARTEX have become increasingly powerful tools enabling effective attacks on exposed infrastructure.
entries.text: Over the last month, the number of Large Language Model (LLM) penetration testing and orchestration frameworks has exploded. Just a few weeks ago, ARTEX — an open source agentic penetration testing system that automates offensive security workflows — was the only framework available. In just the last three days, we have seen over 50 framework families attempt to scan Cloudflare customers globally. The number of Internet Protocol (IP) addresses seen running these frameworks has grown into the thousands and continues to increase daily. The proliferation of these frameworks has significantly changed the status quo in cyber defense: defenders are struggling to keep up with the volumetric nature of these autonomously guided attacks. ARTEX was taken down by its creator Autumn-27 on October 8. (“The malicious exploitation of this tool runs entirely counter to its original intent,” they wrote in Chinese.) But in the month since, the ecosystem has exploded with new fragmented versions of it. There are now over 12,000 repositories, with several hundred unique forks containing lineage from the original repository. Additionally, hundreds of other similar agentic orchestration frameworks have been created since October 8. Daily requests of AI penetration testing (pentesting) and exploitation tools has grown by 30x since October 1. These tools have also begun chaining stolen customer credentials in some of the more complex attacks, such as lateral movement chaining throughout an environmen
entries.title: Adapting to AI penetration testing orchestrators: The Modern Security Model

entries.summary: Spend Management adds opt-in spending caps for Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects, and more products soon. Here is how we built the metering pipeline that turns usage into runtime decisions.
entries.text: Spend controls have been at the top of the list of most requested features from developers building on our developer platform for quite some time now. With more than 10 million developers now building on Cloudflare, this matters more than ever. Although we’ve had usage notifications and budget alerts available to paid plans for a while, this doesn’t solve the problem completely; informing is not the same as controlling. You can now set spending thresholds and choose to have Cloudflare pause activity when those limits are reached, thus avoiding unexpected bills from unplanned usage. Today, we're introducing Spend Management in Beta, for any pay-as-you-go (PayGo) customer, starting with Workers and Durable Objects. Use Spend Management alongside AI Gateway spend limits to manage compute and AI inference costs across your application. AI Gateway already supports per-user and per-model budgets for Workers AI and other AI providers, applied to requests routed through your gateway. How it works You can start using Spend Management using the dashboard, cf CLI, or REST API. In the dashboard, head over to Manage Account > Billing > Spend limits and enable the products for which you want to control spending. When you enable controls on a product, you can define a spending limit, specify a recipient email for notifications, and set one or more alert thresholds. If you configure a recipient email, Cloudflare will send notifications when the evaluated spend reaches one of the thresholds o
entries.title: Introducing Spend Management: Spending limits and alerts for Cloudflare

entries.summary: Cloudflare is building an experimental consensus service using a never-before-deployed consensus algorithm, QuePaxa. In this post we explain how QuePaxa works and why we chose it.
entries.text: Cloudflare recently announced Meerkat, an experimental distributed consensus service designed to manage our internal global control plane. It is powered by a new consensus algorithm published by researchers Tennage & Băsescu et al. called QuePaxa (2023). QuePaxa is an unusual choice; most consensus systems use well-established consensus algorithms like Raft, (Multi-)Paxos or Viewstamped Replication. These algorithms are well understood, have mature implementations, and usually work well. Unfortunately, common consensus algorithms often suffer in wide-area networks with volatile network connectivity and latency, i.e., networks like the Internet, which is where Meerkat runs. These algorithms rely on a single leader process being available and having predictable latency. If the leader goes down, experiences higher latency than usual, or is disconnected, the entire consensus system slows down or becomes unavailable until the leader is replaced. This is unacceptable for Meerkat. Meerkat’s global deployment environment led us to a newer consensus algorithm, QuePaxa, which promises better stability despite volatility, in large part by not relying on a leader to make progress. In this post we’ll explain why we chose QuePaxa and how the QuePaxa algorithm works. What we’re building and why it’s unique Meerkat is a distributed system in which replicas agree upon an ordered log of events, where each event is decided by a consensus algorithm. entries.title: Choosing QuePaxa, an unusual consensus algorithm

entries.summary: Cloudflare is distributing the first $301,300 of the Vite Ecosystem Fund to open source projects and maintainers.
entries.text: Cloudflare is distributing the first $301,300 of the Vite Ecosystem Fund to 44 projects and maintainers across the Vite ecosystem. When VoidZero joined Cloudflare, we committed $1 million to strengthen the open source ecosystem around Vite. This round is just the start. Sponsoring open source has always mattered, but now AI has made funding urgent. AI is changing open source AI has made open source more valuable while triggering more maintainer burnout. Previously, contributing to a project through either an issue or pull request meant you cared about it. In return, maintainers would review and provide feedback. AI changed the social contract of open source. Anyone can now create and submit AI-authored pull requests. The most visible result is the influx of pull requests. As the number of PRs has gone up, the number of maintainers reviewing them has stayed constant. So each maintainer’s workload has grown. During reviews, maintainers often find themselves speaking with an agent and not a person like they used to. If that’s the case, then why not cut out the middleman? Maintainers now have their own agents they can prompt to produce better results since they have more knowledge of the codebase. AI has raised the pressure to produce. It’s made it easier for maintainers to ship features, performance improvements, and bug fixes that would not have been done otherwise. But it’s also made it easy for other projects to do the same. entries.title: Launching the Vite Ecosystem Fund

entries.summary: Cryptographic protocols like Privacy Pass help keep web sites safe from abuse while keeping their users private.
entries.text: The highest priorities for the transition to post-quantum cryptography are the basic building blocks of authenticated key-agreement protocols such as TLS. Without these building blocks in place, secure communication on the Internet will not be possible once cryptographically relevant quantum computers come online. However, today we rely on quantum-vulnerable cryptography for much more than TLS. Privacy Pass is a protocol used by site operators like Cloudflare to help protect applications from abuse. One way we do this is by rate limiting individual clients so that no one client consumes too many of the site's resources. Normally this involves some combination of friction or loss of privacy for users: CAPTCHAs or other challenges to moderate traffic, along with accounts and fingerprinting to identify traffic.Privacy Pass was designed to avoid this tradeoff between friction and privacy. The basic idea is that a client gets issued a number of tokens, which they can redeem in exchange for access to the site. Crucially, each token is unlinkable to the client it was issued to, ensuring the client can use the site as they always had without sacrificing privacy. With 10 years of deployment experience under our belts — using Privacy Pass for applications such as privacy proxies (like iCloud Private Relay) and relays (like Privacy Gateway) — we, along with others, are collaborating to bring the next generation of this technology to the web. One of our goals is to develop more sophistic
entries.title: The post-quantum future of web privacy

entries.summary: AI agents act for millions, but servers see intermediaries that strip user visibility.
entries.text: AI Agents now act on the web for millions of people. To a Site, an Agent can take many forms. It may be indistinguishable from a human user carrying out a task, or it might look like one visitor carrying many Users. This removes the ability for the Site to recognize, serve, and hold accountable the user or users behind the Agent, and causes the Site to face the costs when something goes wrong. This post argues that in order for Sites to maximize the access they provide to Agents, the ecosystem must develop new mechanisms to preserve the relationship between Sites and Users. Traditionally, in Security and Fraud Prevention, that requires three things: Identity, Reputation, and Accountability, allowing Sites to answer: Is the person acting being truthful about who they are? Is that person trustworthy? And who answers for the action? “Personal AI Agents” (“Agents” for short) are automations that take instructions from a human (“User”) and pursue a goal by controlling a cloud computer or browser. They are usually hosted and maintained by an “Operator” as part of a managed service or consumer offering. Examples include Muse from Meta and dots from OpenAI, and more are launching all the time. Agents can potentially take any action online that their User could, without the limits that hold humans back. They don't tire, they run around the clock, they act in parallel, and they put up with friction no person would. Much of the web, from how Sites plan capacity to how they make money, a
entries.title: Agents aren’t humans (but they kinda are)

entries.summary: Personal AI agents have changed how users interact with the web, blurring the lines between automated and human traffic.
entries.text: Personal agents are the intermediary between humans and the Internet, turning a person’s instructions into requests and actions on websites. A customer might ask a personal agent to compare products across your site, find support articles, or complete a purchase. To a site owner, all three interactions show up as automated traffic — and without a clear view of which agents are visiting and what they are doing, it can be difficult to know whether that traffic is helping your business or creating risk. Blocking agents altogether can feel like the safest choice, but it can mean losing customers. Better visibility into agent activity allows you to decide what access makes sense for your site. Today, we’re launching new analytics to help you understand how personal agents access your site on behalf of humans, along with more granular access policies to put those decisions into practice. Together, they let you welcome agents on your own terms, and in ways that support your business. See how agents access your site Knowing which agent is behind a request turns unexplained automated traffic into traffic you can act on with confidence. Cloudflare maintains the largest verified bot directory in the world, and we are now bringing that intelligence into your traffic details. In Security Analytics, the Bot Analysis chart now shows Personal Assistants as a new category, next to Verified Bot, Likely Human, Likely Automated, and Automated. Security teams can select it to see only personal ag
entries.title: See the agents, set the terms: New visibility and control for personal agents

entries.summary: Zero Wire on Cloudflare Radar pairs plain-language briefings with global attack telemetry and remediation steps. Triage critical CVEs faster and decide how to protect your infrastructure.
entries.text: You run security at your organization. It’s 7:00 am, and you’re having breakfast. You receive a ping: a new critical vulnerability has been disclosed. Your team scrambles to compare vendor advisories, read technical research, check which systems run the affected software, and answer familiar questions from the business: are we affected, and what are we doing about it? Another disclosure arrives before that work is finished. AI is changing both the volume and speed of critical vulnerability discovery. It can analyze large codebases at scale and surface deeply nested flaws that may have existed for years without being found through human review. That discovery momentum will put more pressure on security teams to understand the impact of each disclosure on their infrastructure. To help security teams prepare, today we’re introducing Zero Wire: a public vulnerability intelligence feed on Cloudflare Radar, bringing the clarity of a news wire service to critical security developments. It helps security leaders and practitioners understand significant vulnerabilities and decide what to do next. How it works Zero Wire lives inside Cloudflare Radar under the security section. Each briefing brings together a plain-language explanation of the vulnerability, who should investigate it, recommended actions, and links to the evidence and vendor guidance. The format is deliberately simple: an index card with what you need to know, without the drama. A CISO should be able to understand the is
entries.title: Introducing Zero Wire, a hub for investigating critical Internet vulnerabilities

entries.summary: Zone setting changes used to rebuild entire DNS zones, even ones with tens of millions of records.
entries.text: When I last wrote about our DNS propagation pipeline in 2022, the Zone Builder received about 250 DNS record changes per second. Today it receives about 700, nearly three times as many, plus about 100 other events, such as zone setting changes. However, the number of events was never the real problem. The problem was the kind of work some of those events needed, and how that work grows with the size of a zone. Some zones now hold more than 20 million records, and we expect them to keep growing toward hundreds of millions. Each event starts a clock that measures how long it takes us to turn that change into data our authoritative DNS servers can use. We call that work a build. A build reads the current database state, converts it into the format used at the edge, and writes any changes to Quicksilver. In 2022, per-record builds were 150 times faster than full builds on average. On a test zone with one million records, per-record builds were 4,250 times faster. We ended that post with the obvious next step: do the same thing for zone settings. Why doesn't the Zone Builder just rebuild the setting that changed? It should, and that is where we ended up. However, proving when it was safe took most of the work. A record event identifies what changed. A zone event can come from many Cloudflare products, may not say why the zone changed, and can alter data shared by several zones with the same name. Choosing too much work wastes capacity. Choosing too little can leave stale or incorr
entries.title: How we halved DNS build delay and cut memory use by 85%

entries.summary: Four, just four: that’s the key to break into any unpatched connection on the Internet that is using eMudhra certificates.
entries.text: On October 19, 2026, we learned about eMudhra’s eight shockingly weak keys: where eMudhra was trusted to pick a 115-digit number for their virtual combination lock protecting the Internet, they picked the number 4. Not even four digits, just the number 4. The other seven keys were similarly weak: 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237. The next day, we wrote a blog post on the immediate action we took to mitigate this leak, and what customers needed to do on their end to stay secure. Now, we are sharing a more in-depth follow up on the evidence we’ve seen of exploitation, and the progress seen on visitors patching their systems. Let's start with the scale of the problem. A certificate authority (CA) with weak keys this serious is unprecedented, and the potential consequences are significant. While there have been plenty of compromised certification authorities in the past (such as DigiNotar, TÜRKTRUST, and TrustWave), access to their keys has always been contained to a degree; these incidents gave a limited set of attackers or organizations the ability to issue fraudulent certificates. The eMudhra incident is fundamentally different; the affected intermediate private keys could be recovered almost instantly by anyone from the public certificates themselves. Anyone can independently recover these same signing keys and create certificates for any domain that an unpatched client not enforcing Certificate Transparency would accept. eMudhra announced they’re exiting the public CA busi
entries.title: 4 real? Tracking exploitation and patching of eMudhra’s weak keys

entries.summary: Public traffic to private origins, with WAF, bot management, caching, and Workers, is now available to every customer with Cloudflare One connectivity.
entries.text: Today, Cloudflare services for private origins is generally available. Point a proxied DNS record at a private IP, and Cloudflare reaches the origin over your existing Cloudflare One connection. Your origin stays private, while web application firewall (WAF), caching, bot management, and Workers work just as they do for public origins. In June, we launched this capability in closed beta to address a problem we kept hearing from customers: Their internal APIs, AI agent backends, MCP servers, and operational tools weren’t built to face the Internet, but those services still need to accept requests from partners, customers, or agents over the Internet. Before the beta, putting Cloudflare in front of these services meant exposing a public IP, opening a firewall port, or running cloudflared alongside the origin. Those requirements often left private applications without the same protections and controls they used for public applications, including WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching, traffic acceleration, rewrites, and Workers. What is generally available today During the closed beta, eligible customers requested access through their account team. Today, we’re opening access beyond that beta group. Point a proxied A or AAAA record at a private IP, and Cloudflare’s application services work as they do for public origins: WAF and managed rules Bot management Rate limiting Caching Transform and rewrite rules Workers Some limitations remain. entries.title: Cloudflare services for private origins is now generally available

entries.summary: Cloudflare mitigated over 8,200 DDoS attacks per hour in Q3 2026 as attackers shifted to shorter, high-frequency strikes.
entries.text: Welcome to the 26th edition of Cloudflare's DDoS Threat Report. This edition covers the third quarter of 2026 — July, August, and September — and returns the series to its quarterly cadence following the combined H1 2026 volume. The analysis is produced by Cloudforce One, Cloudflare's Threat Intelligence organization, providing a comprehensive analysis of the evolving threat landscape of Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks based on data from the Cloudflare network. Key insights Short-burst, low-bandwidth attacks lasting under 10 minutes and 1 Gbps surged by 208%. Conversely, hyper-volumetric attacks exceeding 1 Tbps plummeted by nearly 69% from Q2, possibly a reflection of law enforcement actions against four major Internet of Things (IoT) botnets earlier in the year. However, variants continue to emerge, proving that IoT botnets remain a durable, high-volume threat to network infrastructure. Threat actors dramatically shifted their reflection and amplification tactics, abruptly abandoning CLDAP floods, which collapsed by 99.5% quarter-over-quarter. Instead, attackers pivoted heavily toward other connectionless protocols, driving a 215% surge in DNS amplification and a 122% increase in general UDP floods. Attack targets broadened significantly across both industries and geographies, with the United States reclaiming the most-attacked position from China. Canada and Israel experienced sharp spikes in targeted attacks — jumping 10 and 7 spots respectively — while juggl
entries.title: Cloudflare DDoS Threat Report 2026 Q3: More swarms, fewer giants
